# Asparagus Growth

[Someone on the internet is claiming that asparagus shoots grow 10" in a 24 hour period](
https://www.reddit.com/r/AskReddit/comments/9v1ynv/whats_your_favorite_fun_fact/e98pqb1/). 
In order to test this theory, you go to your asparagus patch and measure each new shoot from each plant. 
You measure its length (in inches) at 8AM on the day it appeared and then again at 8AM the next day, subtracting to document the amount of growth. 

As each plant produces multiple shoots, you end up with a sample of 85 measurements. The sample mean is 9.53 inches, with a sample standard deviation of 2.4 inches.

## Experimental Design

- What is the research question? That is, what do you hope to determine by collecting data?

> Does asparagus grow 10" in a 24 hour period?

- What is the observational unit?

> A shoot of asparagus

- What type of variable is this? Categorical or Quantitative?

> Quantitative

- If you were conducting a hypothesis test, what would $H_0$ and $H_A$ be?

> $H_0$: $\mu = 10$
> $H_A$: $\mu \neq 10$

- If you were using a confidence interval to conduct a test, what value would need to be outside the interval to reject the null hypothesis?

> 10"

## Calculations

- What is your sample statistic?

> $\overline X = 9.53$

- What is the standard error? 

```{r}
#| error: true
(asparagus_se <- 2.4 / sqrt(85))
```

- Does the central limit theorem apply to this data? Why or why not?

> Yes, the central limit theorem applies, because we have more than 20 observations of continuous data.

## Confidence Intervals

- What formula should you use for a 95% confidence interval?  Provide the value of any constants you will use (e.g. multipliers).


> Estimate +/- Multiplier * SE(Estimate)
> Multiplier = `{r} qnorm(.975)`


- Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the amount asparagus grows in a 24h period.

```{r}
#| error: true

asparagus_ci <- 9.53 + c(-1,1)*qnorm(.975)*asparagus_se
asparagus_ci
```


- What is your confidence level? What level of $\alpha$ corresponds to this confidence level?

> 95% confidence, so $\alpha = 0.05$ 


- Interpret your confidence interval in the context of the problem.


> We are 95% confident that on average, a shoot of asparagus can grow between `{r} asparagus_ci[1]` and `{r} asparagus_ci[2]` inches in a 24 hour period. 


## Hypothesis Test

- Calculate $Z^\ast$, the critical value for your hypothesis test.

```{r}
#| error: true
(asparagus_z <- (9.53 - 10)/asparagus_se)
```

- Calculate your p-value using `pnorm`

```{r}
#| error: true
(asparagus_p <- pnorm(asparagus_z)*2)
```

- What is your conclusion, based on your p-value?


> With a p-value of 0.071, we do not have sufficient evidence to reject $H_0: \mu = 10$; it is plausible that we could have observed our data when, on average, asparagus grows $\mu = 10$ inches in a 24 hour period. 

- Does your conclusion match the conclusion you would draw by interpreting your confidence interval? Why or why not?


> Yes. Our confidence interval contains 10, which suggests that it is plausible for $\mu = 10$. We should not reject $H_0$. 



# Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)

On TV, CPR is seemingly more successful than it is in real life, where about 45% of people who receive CPR are at least temporarily resuscitated, and only 10% survive to discharge from the hospital. 
A group of doctors collected data on CPR survival rates in medical dramas, examining 88 episodes which aired between July 2008 and April 2009. 
They documented 70 CPR attempts; 32 succeeded in temporarily resuscitating the patient. 
Attempts to determine the percent successfully discharged from the hospital failed, as this is not a part of the plot line in most TV dramas.

## Experimental Design

- What is the research question? That is, what do the doctors want to determine?

> Do medical dramas demonstrate a higher rate of temporary resuscitation when CPR is used than occurs in real life?

- What is the observational unit?

> Patients on whom CPR is attempted in a medical drama

- What type of variable is this? Categorical or Quantitative?

> Categorical -- whether they are temporarily resuscitated (1) or not (0)

- If you were conducting a hypothesis test, what would $H_0$ and $H_A$ be using appropriate mathematical notation?

> $H_0$: $\pi = 0.45$
> $H_A$: $\pi \neq 0.45$ or $\pi > 0.45$ -- both are reasonable here, though the latter requires a one-sided interval and test. 

- If you were using a confidence interval to conduct a test, what value would need to be outside the interval to reject the null hypothesis?

> 0.45

## Calculations

- What is your sample statistic?

> $\overline X = `{r} 32/70`$

- What is the standard error? 

```{r}
#| error: true

cpr_stat <- 32/70
(cpr_se <- sqrt(cpr_stat*(1-cpr_stat)/70))
```

- Does the central limit theorem apply to this data? Why or why not?

> Yes, we have more than 5 successes and more than 5 failures, with categorical data, so the central limit theorem applies. 

## Confidence Interval

- What formula should you use for a 95% confidence interval?  Provide the value of any constants you will use (e.g. multipliers).

> Estimate +/- Multiplier * SE(Estimate)
> Multiplier = `{r} qnorm(.975)`


- Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the amount asparagus grows in a 24h period.

```{r}
#| error: true

cpr_ci <- cpr_stat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(.975)*cpr_se
cpr_ci
```


- What is your confidence level? What level of $\alpha$ corresponds to this confidence level?

> 95%, which corresponds to $\alpha = 0.05$. 


- Interpret your confidence interval in the context of the problem.


> We are 95% confident that the population average temporary resuscitation rate when CPR is performed in a medical drama is between 34% and 57%. As the temporary resuscitation rate in real life is estimated to be 45%, it is plausible that medical dramas represent the temporary resuscitation rate accurately. 


## Hypothesis Test

- Calculate $Z^\ast$, the critical value for your hypothesis test.

```{r}
#| error: true
(cpr_z <- (cpr_stat-0.45)/cpr_se)
```

- Calculate your p-value using `pnorm`

```{r}
#| error: true
(cpr_p <- pnorm(cpr_z, lower.tail = F)*2)
```

- What is your conclusion, based on your p-value?


> With a p-value of .905, we fail to reject the null hypothesis that $\pi = 0.45$. It is completely plausible that we would observe data as or more extreme than what our sample showed with a population CPR temporary resuscitation rate of 45%. 

- Does your conclusion match the conclusion you would draw by interpreting your confidence interval? Why or why not?


> Yes, the conclusion matches. 45% is almost exactly at the center of the 95% confidence interval.
